blocks.prompt: The Gray Baby That Turned Into a Swan
blocks.text: A baby swan is called a cygnet. Cygnets do not look like their parents. They are gray and fuzzy, like little dust balls with feet. Their mom and dad are big and white and smooth. The cygnets swim in a line behind their mom. When they get tired, they climb onto her back. She carries them across the water while they rest. All summer the cygnets grow. Their gray fluff falls out. New white feathers push in. By the time they are one year old, they are white too. Now they look just like their parents.

blocks.prompt: More Bones Than a Giraffe
blocks.text: Look at a giraffe. Now look at a swan. The giraffe is one of the tallest animals on Earth, and its neck has seven bones in it. Your neck has seven bones too. So does a mouse. Almost every mammal gets seven, no matter the size. A swan does not follow that rule. A swan's neck holds around twenty-five bones, more than any other bird. That is why the neck bends into such a smooth curve, and why it can fold, stretch, and swing in almost any direction. The long neck is not for show. Ducks feed in shallow water, because a duck can only reach so far down. A swan tips its body forward, points its tail at the sky, and reaches its whole neck under the surface. It pulls up plants growing in mud that no duck can touch. This is called upending. The swan does not dive. It just brings its mouth to the food, and leaves the rest of itself on top.

answers: seven

tipping the body forward and reaching the neck under the water to feed
(inference: the swan can reach plants in deeper mud without diving or swimming down)

blocks.prompt: Cob, Pen, and Cygnet
blocks.text: A pair of swans will often stay together for years, sometimes for their whole lives. The male is called a cob. The female is called a pen. Together they build a nest that looks like a small haystack at the edge of the water, piled up from reeds and grass until it stands well above the waterline. The pen lays her eggs there, usually four to seven of them, and sits on them for around five weeks. When the cygnets hatch, both parents guard them. This is when swans earn their reputation. A cob will lower his head, arch his wings up over his back, and come at anything that gets close, hissing the whole way. He is not being mean. He is standing between his family and whatever is coming. Flying is harder for a swan than it looks. A trumpeter swan can weigh as much as a large dog, and a heavy bird cannot simply leap into the air. It has to run. The swan beats its wings and sprints across the surface of the water, slapping it with both feet, for a hundred feet or more before it finally lifts. Once it is up, the same weight becomes an advantage. A swan can hold a steady line for hundreds of miles. Tundra swans fly from the Arctic to the coasts of the United States every fall, and back again every spring.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Black swans are native to Australia
They have red bills and dark feathers
Europeans thought all swans were white
Willem de Vlamingh saw them in 1697
The Swan River in Perth is named for them
A black swan now means an event nobody saw coming

blocks.prompt: The Bird That Was Impossible
blocks.text: For most of European history, everyone knew what a swan was: a white bird. Not usually white. Not mostly white. White, the way water is wet. Roman writers used the phrase 'a rare bird, like a black swan' to mean a thing that does not exist. If you wanted to say something was impossible, you said it was a black swan, and everyone understood you. In 1697 a Dutch captain named Willem de Vlamingh sailed up a river on the west coast of Australia and saw black swans. Whole flocks of them, gliding around with red bills and dark feathers, entirely real and completely uninterested in European opinion. He named the river the Swan River. The city of Perth stands on it now. He was not the first person to see them. Aboriginal Australians had lived alongside black swans for tens of thousands of years and had names and stories for them. De Vlamingh was only the first person to carry the news back to Europe, where it landed like a small explosion. Nothing about the birds had changed. What changed was the confidence. Europeans had been certain about black swans for roughly two thousand years, and their certainty had been built on a large pile of evidence: every swan anyone had ever seen was white. The evidence was real. The conclusion was still wrong, because nobody had looked at Australia yet. That is why the phrase survived, but flipped. Today a black swan means the opposite of what it used to. It means a rare event nobody saw coming, the kind that only looks obvious afterward. The birds themselves are common in Australia, unbothered and loud, and they became a lesson in how not to think. The lesson holds beyond birds. No amount of white swans proves that black ones cannot exist. One black swan settles it forever.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Trumpeter swan: Cygnus buccinator
Heaviest bird in North America
Only 69 known in the lower 48 in 1935
Over 63,000 counted in 2015
Mute swans were brought to America in the 1800s
Mute swans are now controlled as an invasive species

blocks.prompt: Two Swans, Two Opposite Rescues
blocks.text: In 1935, someone counted the trumpeter swans left in the lower forty-eight states of America and came back with a number: sixty-nine. Not sixty-nine flocks. Sixty-nine birds, nearly all of them huddled in one warm-spring valley in Montana called Red Rock Lakes. The trumpeter is the heaviest bird in North America. A big male can pass thirty pounds and stretch his wings across eight feet. That size had been the problem. Swan skins sold well in Europe, the down went into powder puffs and quilts, the long wing feathers were cut into writing quills, and the meat was worth taking. For two centuries the Hudson's Bay Company shipped swan skins out of North America by the tens of thousands. A bird that needs a hundred feet of open water just to get airborne is not hard to shoot. What saved the trumpeter was partly law and partly luck. The Migratory Bird Treaty Act of 1918 made the killing illegal. Red Rock Lakes became a refuge in 1935 specifically for the survivors. Then, in the 1950s, biologists flying over Alaska found something nobody had expected: thousands of trumpeter swans, quietly getting on with it in country too remote to have been hunted out. The species had never been as close to the edge as the count suggested. It had simply been counted in the wrong place. From those two populations, the trumpeter came back. Birds were moved, released, and protected across the Midwest. A 2015 survey counted more than sixty-three thousand. It is one of the clearest conservation wins on the continent. Now hold that story next to a second one. The mute swan, the orange-billed bird with the black knob and the perfect curved neck, is not native to North America. It was brought over in the 1800s to decorate the ponds of estates and city parks, and some of the birds escaped. Mute swans eat several pounds of aquatic plants a day, tear up beds that native fish and ducks depend on, and drive other waterbirds off nesting grounds by force. In parts of the Atlantic coast, wildlife agencies now control mute swan numbers on purpose, and every time they do, people who love the bird object, loudly and sincerely. Both birds are swans. Both are beautiful in exactly the same way. One is protected at great public expense, and one is removed at great public expense, and the difference between them has nothing to do with the birds. It is about where they belong, and who decided to move them.
